title: How do you solve a private equity case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete private equity case guide: entry price, debt, value creation, exit and returns, worked through a gym chain buyout with a money multiple and IRR.
hook: You solve a private equity case by working out whether the deal earns the fund the return it needs: what equity goes in, what equity comes out at the exit, and the yearly rate that connects them. The market, the company and the value-creation plan all matter because they feed that one calculation. This guide works through a gym chain buyout, step by step, including the downside cases that decide whether you say yes.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a private equity case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: buying a gym chain
  • Where the return comes from
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a private equity case

A private equity fund wants to buy a company, improve it and sell it, typically within three to seven years. The prompt is usually "should the fund buy this company?" or "is this price worth paying?" It looks like an M&A case, with one big difference: the fund has no existing business to combine with, so there are no synergies. The return has to come from growing profits, paying down debt and selling at a good price.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Start with the finish line:

What return does the fund need, and over how many years?

Then work through four questions:

  • Is the market attractive? Size and growth, margins, barriers to entry, and how it behaves in a downturn.
  • Is the company strong? Its position against competitors, recent performance, the management team.
  • How can the fund add value? Grow revenue, raise margins, buy smaller add-on companies.
  • Can the fund exit well? Who would buy it, at what multiple, and when.

The calculation that ties it together: money multiple = equity at exit ÷ equity at entry. The money multiple converts to a yearly return, or IRR. Two benchmarks worth knowing: tripling your money in six years is about 20% a year, and doubling it in four years is about 19% a year. If there is no credible buyer at the exit, there is no deal. The private equity framework covers each branch in more depth.

A fully worked example: buying a gym chain

The prompt: a fund can buy a chain of 80 gyms that makes $20M of EBITDA for 8 times EBITDA. It needs about 20% a year over five years. Should it buy? The figures are illustrative.

Step 1: the entry

  • Price: 8 × $20M = $160M.
  • The fund borrows 60% of the price ($96M) and puts in $64M of its own equity.

Step 2: the plan

Opening new gyms and modest price rises could lift EBITDA to $30M in five years. The business also uses its cash flow to repay debt, from $96M down to $60M. Ask whether the cash flow can really fund both the new gyms and $36M of debt repayment: if not, one of the two assumptions has to give.

Step 3: the exit

Assume the fund sells at the same 8 times multiple: 8 × $30M = $240M. After repaying the remaining $60M of debt, the fund receives $180M.

Step 4: the return

$180M ÷ $64M ≈ 2.8 times the money. Over five years that is about 23% a year, because 1.23 multiplied by itself five times is about 2.8. That beats the 20% target.

Step 5: test the downside

ScenarioExit valueEquity outMultipleYearly return
Plan: $30M EBITDA, 8x$240M$180M2.8xAbout 23%
Weaker growth: $25M, 8x$200M$140M2.2xAbout 17%
Lower multiple: $30M, 7x$210M$150M2.3xAbout 19%
No growth: $20M, 7x$140M$80M1.25xAbout 5%

The deal clears the target only if the growth plan delivers and the exit multiple holds. The last row shows why debt cuts both ways: the business would still be worth $140M, but after $60M of debt the fund barely gets its money back.

Step 6: the maximum price

Work backwards from the target. A 20% yearly return over five years means multiplying the money by about 2.5 (1.2 to the power of 5 ≈ 2.49). With $180M out, the most equity the fund can put in is $180M ÷ 2.49 ≈ $72M. Add the $96M of debt and the maximum price is about $168M, or roughly 8.4 times EBITDA. So the fund has very little room to bid higher.

Step 7: the recommendation

Yes, at 8 times EBITDA the deal returns about 2.8 times the fund's money, around 23% a year, against a 20% target. But it depends on EBITDA growing to $30M: at $25M the return drops to about 17%. I'd buy only if due diligence confirms the new-gym plan and that cash flow can fund it while repaying debt, and I would not pay more than about 8.4 times. The main risk is member churn in a downturn, so I'd test how membership held up in the last recession.

Where the return comes from

Interviewers like candidates who can say why a deal works. Split the fund's $116M gain ($180M out minus $64M in) into its sources:

  • EBITDA growth: $10M more EBITDA at 8 times adds $80M to the value of the business.
  • Debt paydown: $36M of debt repaid moves $36M of value from lenders to the fund.
  • Multiple change: zero here, because the fund buys and sells at 8 times.

$80M + $36M + $0 = $116M. The value of the business rose 50% ($160M to $240M), but the fund's equity grew 2.8 times, because it was bought largely with borrowed money. That is the core logic of a leveraged buyout, and the reason the downside rows above fall so fast.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer stays qualitative:

Gyms are a growing market, the company has a good brand, and the fund could open more sites, so it looks attractive.

A strong answer gets to the return early and names the swing factor:

Let me work out the return: equity in, equity out, and the yearly rate that connects them.
The deal clears the 20% target only if EBITDA reaches $30M, so the growth plan is the key risk.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Never calculating a return. Get to equity in and equity out within the first third of the case.
  2. Forgetting the exit. Who buys the company, and at what multiple? Assuming the multiple rises is optimistic; flat is the safer default.
  3. Ignoring debt. It boosts the return when things go well and wipes out equity when they do not.
  4. Not testing the plan. Run at least one downside: weaker growth or a lower exit multiple.
  5. Recommending a deal because the market is growing. A great market at too high a price is a bad deal.

Practise with these prompts

Quick maths: a fund puts in $50M and gets $100M back after four years. Roughly what yearly return is that?

Show the answer

A 2 times multiple. By the rule of 72, money doubles in four years at about 72 ÷ 4 = 18% a year. The exact figure is about 19%, since 1.19 to the power of 4 ≈ 2.0.

Quick maths: a company is bought for $100M with $60M of debt. Five years later it sells for $140M and $30M of debt remains. What is the money multiple?

Show the answer

Equity in: $100M − $60M = $40M. Equity out: $140M − $30M = $110M. Multiple: $110M ÷ $40M = 2.75 times, about 22% a year, even though the business's value grew only 40%.

Should a private equity fund buy a regional chain of veterinary clinics?

Show the answer
  • Market: pet ownership and spending trends, how fragmented the market is, resilience in a downturn.
  • The company: profit per clinic, best against worst, vet recruitment and retention.
  • Value creation: buying independent clinics at lower multiples, shared purchasing, adding services such as diagnostics.
  • Deal and exit: price, debt, return against target; buyers at exit, such as larger groups or another fund.

Where to start: the return at this price under a sensible plan, then whether buying smaller clinics can lift it.

The trap: ignoring that vets, not buildings, are the scarce resource.
